# Personal Context

## Who I Am

I'm a Computer Science student at the University at Buffalo. Most of my time is spent building software, but what keeps me interested isn't the technology itself. It's the process of taking a messy problem that frustrates people and turning it into something that actually works.

I didn't get into programming because I was fascinated by algorithms or computer architecture. I got into it because I liked solving problems. Over time I realized that software is one of the few fields where a small group of people can build something that thousands of others use every day.

A lot of students build projects because they're good resume material. I usually start with a problem that annoys me or someone around me. The project becomes an excuse to solve it.

## What I Care About

I'm interested in systems that remove friction from people's lives. The problems that excite me most are the ones that seem small on the surface but waste thousands of hours when nobody fixes them.

I care about tools, infrastructure, developer productivity, automation, and increasingly AI systems that can take action instead of simply generating text. I think there is a huge opportunity to build software that helps people accomplish real-world tasks rather than just answer questions.

One thing I find interesting is that many of the best engineering problems are invisible. Nobody notices when a system is reliable, when a deployment goes smoothly, or when a workflow saves five minutes. But those improvements compound across hundreds or thousands of users.

If money and constraints didn't matter, I would probably spend my time building autonomous systems that solve practical problems in education, accessibility, and infrastructure. I'm more interested in useful technology than flashy technology.

## My Values & How I Work

I optimize for usefulness.

A lot of projects are technically impressive but don't solve a meaningful problem. I'd rather build something simple that people actually use than something complicated that nobody needs.

When making engineering decisions, I usually favor reliability and maintainability over cleverness. The best solution is often not the most technically sophisticated one. It's the one that other people can understand, operate, and improve.

I also care a lot about ownership. If I take responsibility for a problem, I become obsessed with solving it. I don't enjoy leaving things half-finished or "good enough" when I know there's a fix.

One thing that separates me from many people I've worked with is that I have a hard time walking away from unsolved problems. When something breaks, I want to understand why. When a design doesn't feel right, I keep iterating until it does. Sometimes that's frustrating, but it's also the reason I've been able to solve problems that initially seemed impossible.

## Project Stories

### Next Up

Next Up started because I saw how inefficient office hours could be. Students would wait without knowing where they were in line, teaching assistants would manually manage queues, and everyone involved lost time.

The technical challenges weren't the hardest part. The difficult part was designing a system that people would actually trust enough to replace an existing process. If students didn't trust the queue or if teaching assistants found it inconvenient, the project would fail regardless of the implementation.

The biggest lesson I learned was that software adoption is often harder than software development. Building features is relatively straightforward. Building something that changes behavior is much harder.

### UB Hacking CMS

This is probably the project I'm most proud of.

Every year, student developers rebuilt large parts of UB Hacking's infrastructure from scratch. That meant institutional knowledge disappeared, engineering time was wasted, and new teams repeatedly solved the same problems.

The goal wasn't just to build a website. The goal was to build a platform that future teams could inherit.

One of the hardest decisions was choosing between maximizing flexibility and keeping the system maintainable. It's tempting to add endless customization options, but that usually creates complexity that future developers have to manage. I spent a lot of time thinking about what not to build.

The project taught me that good engineering isn't always about creating new features. Sometimes it's about removing future work.

### ResQme

ResQme came from a simple question: what happens when communication infrastructure disappears?

Most modern applications assume internet connectivity. During emergencies, that's often the first thing that becomes unreliable.

The challenge wasn't building a messaging application. The challenge was designing a system that could continue functioning when many of the assumptions modern software depends on were gone.

Working on ResQme made me think differently about reliability. It's easy to build systems that work under ideal conditions. It's much harder to build systems that work when everything starts failing.

## Goals & What I Want From Opportunities

I apply to internships, hackathons, and programs because they expose me to problems I wouldn't encounter on my own.

A successful internship isn't one where I spend a summer implementing tickets. It's one where I leave understanding how strong engineering teams operate, how large systems are built, and how experienced engineers make decisions.

A successful hackathon isn't necessarily one where I win. It's one where I build something I couldn't have built by myself and learn from people who think differently than I do.

Long term, I want to become the kind of engineer who can take ownership of ambiguous problems and drive them from idea to production.

## Strengths & Working Style

My biggest strength is persistence.

When I encounter a difficult bug, a system failure, or an unfamiliar problem, I rarely give up quickly. I become fixated on understanding what's happening and finding a solution.

In teams, I naturally gravitate toward ownership roles. If there's a problem that nobody is handling, I tend to pick it up. If a project lacks structure, I usually help create it.

I work well under ambiguity because I'm comfortable learning as I go. Most interesting problems don't come with clear instructions.

I also value feedback. Some of my biggest improvements as an engineer have come from having my assumptions challenged by teammates, mentors, and open-source maintainers.

## Beyond Tech

Outside of coding, I spend a lot of time organizing events, mentoring students, and helping build communities through UB Hacking.

I enjoy environments where people are building ambitious things and sharing ideas. A lot of my favorite conversations are with people who approach problems completely differently than I do.

My communication style is direct and practical. I prefer clear explanations over polished buzzwords. I'd rather talk about what actually happened than what sounds impressive.

At the end of the day, I'm motivated by building useful things, solving difficult problems, and continuously improving. The technology changes. That part stays the same.

Who are we?

Our mission is to scale intelligence to serve humanity. We’re training and deploying frontier models for developers and enterprises who are building AI systems to power magical experiences like content generation, semantic search, RAG, and agents. We believe that our work is instrumental to the widespread adoption of AI.

We obsess over what we build. Each one of us is responsible for contributing to increasing the capabilities of our models and the value they drive for our customers. We like to work hard and move fast to do what’s best for our customers.

Cohere is a team of researchers, engineers, designers, and more, who are passionate about their craft. Each person is one of the best in the world at what they do. We believe that a diverse range of perspectives is a requirement for building great products.

Join us on our mission and shape the future!

Why this role?

This role is for students who are excited about building the next generation of machine learning models and NLP products. Our SWE roles can cover creating datasets for machine learning, scaling the pods to serve our API, or even building out new security features on our platform. We don't distinguish much between interns and full-time employees, and you’ll have plenty of opportunities to push code to production. You'll have full autonomy and ownership over high-impact work, and will be backed by the support of an incredible team or leaders & mentors.

Join us at a pivotal moment, shape what we build, and wear multiple hats!
We're currently hiring for multiple teams and roles, including Frontend, Backend, Full-stack, and Infrastructure roles. We'll take your interests & experience into account throughout the application process.
Our recruitment process will begin in the upcoming weeks, and we will be carefully reviewing applications and assessing potential candidates for our internships. Should we find a suitable match with your qualifications and our requirements, we will be in touch to discuss the opportunity further and to advance your application to the next stage.

Please Note: To be eligible for this position, you should be currently enrolled in a post-secondary program and available for a full-time 3-6 month internship, co-op, or research work term.

As a Software Engineering Intern, you will:

Ship delightful experiences for our user-facing products, meticulously crafting code for browsers or server code.

Build features for the API platform that directly impact users.

Design and implement robust data pipelines (crawlers, storage, filters).

Design and implement scalable services or infrastructure for machine learning development.

Build internal tooling (CI/CD, dev utilities) to move faster together.

Build tech writing skills through maintaining and contributing to technical documentation, both internal and external facing.

Keep up with the cutting edge and adopt new technologies to improve performance and reliability across Cohere.

If some of the above doesn’t line up perfectly with your experience, we still encourage you to apply!
